extracted.intended_audience: EPA decisionmakers, regulators, environmental lawyers, scientists, and public commenters engaged in CAA section 202(a) endangerment determinations and related rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the Administrator evaluates whether emissions of well-mixed greenhouse gases 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare' under Clean Air Act §202(a), including evidentiary, temporal, sectoral, and statutory-interpretation considerations. Applies to preparing or reviewing EPA endangerment findings and supporting technical assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright-line quantitative threshold; exercise Administrator judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The endangerment test under CAA section 202(a) does not require the Administrator to identify a bright line, quantitative threshold above which a positive endangerment finding can be made; the statutory language explicitly calls upon the Administrator to use her judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Administrator's decision may be qualitative and based on overall judgment rather than a single numerical metric. Do not demand a single cutoff value per risk category. The assessment should explain the reasoning used in forming the judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total weight of scientific evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Base the finding on the total weight of scientific evidence linking human emissions and resulting elevated atmospheric concentrations of the six well-mixed greenhouse gases to observed global and regional temperature increases and other climate changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and synthesize multiple lines of evidence (observations, modeling, assessment literature). The evidence should be robust and compelling in aggregate; supporting materials (TSD, Response to Comments) should be referenced for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad scope of impacts to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not limit consideration to any one element of human health, economic sector, region, or aspect of the natural environment; the Administrator bases the finding on risks and impacts across all climate-sensitive elements of public health and welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider impacts across many sectors and domains rather than isolating a single endpoint. Explicitly state which sectors and endpoints were examined and why the totality supports or does not support an endangerment finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated risk categories to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the major risk categories described in the TSD, which include: human health, air quality, food production and agriculture, forestry, water resources, sea level rise and coastal areas, the energy sector, infrastructure and settlements, and ecosystems and wildlife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each listed category, summarize available evidence of present and projected impacts and their relevance to public health or welfare. Use the TSD categories as the organizing framework when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not place primacy on most-studied/most-quantified impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator is not necessarily placing the greatest weight on those risks and impacts which have been the subject of the most study or quantification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that less-quantified but potentially serious impacts merit consideration; avoid equating lack of quantification with lack of importance. Explain how less-quantified evidence was weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider both potential benefits and adverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the variation in risks and impacts is that rising greenhouse gases can bring about potential benefits to public health and welfare in addition to adverse risks; potential benefits are taken into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify any potential benefits (e.g., CO2 fertilization, modest warming benefits) and weigh them against harms to the extent magnitudes can be quantified or characterized. Document directional trends where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple causal pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Because greenhouse gas buildup can cause effects via multiple pathways (e.g., elevated CO2 concentrations, temperature increases, precipitation changes, sea level rise, changes in extreme events), these multiple pathways must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each relevant pathway and how it contributes to sectoral impacts; do not conflate or ignore distinct mechanisms. Where pathways have opposing effects (e.g., CO2 fertilization vs. temperature/precipitation stress), present balanced consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative balancing of sectoral risks and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator has balanced and weighed the varying risks and effects for each sector, judging whether there is a pattern across the sector that supports an endangerment finding; in all these cases the judgment is largely qualitative and not reducible to precise metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a sector-by-sector narrative that explains the directional evidence, relative weight, and whether evidence trends toward net harm or benefit. Make clear when conclusions are qualitative and why quantification is infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate timeframe for analysis (current and future conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both current and future conditions must be considered; the endangerment period of analysis should extend from the current time to the next several decades, and in some cases to the end of this century, consistent with atmospheric lifetimes and climate effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select time horizons aligned with gas lifetimes and plausible projection capability; justify chosen horizons and relate them to assessed impacts (near-term vs long-term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize and incorporate uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that some aspects of climate science and projected impacts are more certain than others: knowledge strongest for recent, large-scale changes; uncertainty increases at smaller regional scales and for longer-term projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe where uncertainty is high vs low, how it affects confidence in conclusions, and whether uncertainties change the weight of evidence. Where appropriate, discuss ranges of plausible outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address varying levels of quantification across sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: In some sectors, future impacts can be quantified; in others only qualitative direction-of-change descriptions may be possible. Low-probability, high-impact outcomes (known unknowns) are possible though may not be explicitly assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which impacts are quantitatively estimated and which are qualitatively characterized; discuss implications of potential low-probability/high-impact events even if they cannot be precisely assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider direct temperature effects on health, including heat-related mortality/morbidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate evidence that unusually hot days and heat waves are becoming more frequent, that heat is a leading cause of weather-related deaths, and that projected warming will increase heat-related mortality and morbidity—especially among vulnerable groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document observed trends, projections of heat-wave frequency/intensity, and epidemiological findings (e.g., heat-related death/morbidity rates). Identify and discuss populations at special risk (elderly, very young, chronically ill, outdoor workers, those without air conditioning, socially isolated, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate air quality effects (ozone and particulate matter) using modeling and key metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how climate change modifies ozone precursor emissions, chemistry, transport and removal, and use models/observations to assess projected changes in summertime surface ozone (e.g., changes in maximum daily 8-hour average ozone concentrations) and uncertainties for particulate matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regional/global model comparisons to estimate changes (EPA cites 2–8 ppb increases averaged over summer for many regions, with larger peak-episode increases). Describe spatial heterogeneity (some regions may see little change or decreases) and the public-health implications of projected changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess health impacts of changes in extreme weather events and vulnerability factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider increased risk of deaths, injuries, infectious diseases, and stress-related disorders associated with more frequent/severe extreme weather (heavy precipitation, floods, tropical cyclone intensity) and account for population vulnerability and preparedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference IPCC and other assessments on links between extreme events and health outcomes (e.g., drowning from storm surge, waterborne disease after floods). Discuss social/environmental determinants of vulnerability (age, income, preparedness, health-sector response).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider climate-sensitive diseases and aeroallergen changes, noting directional support and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate potential increases in food- and water-borne pathogens, changes in vector ranges (e.g., ticks), and impacts of CO2 and temperature on pollen and aeroallergen production, while acknowledging current scientific uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize available studies on pathogen-temperature relationships, vector habitat shifts, and pollen production. Note where evidence is directional rather than definitive and explicitly state how much weight these lines of evidence receive in the overall finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly consider vulnerable populations in public health assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Place weight on the fact that certain groups—including children, the elderly, and the poor—are most vulnerable to climate-related health effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify vulnerable subpopulations in each sectoral assessment and discuss differential exposures, susceptibilities, and adaptive capacity. Use vulnerability as a factor in weighing endangerment risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory interpretation: include indirect health effects mediated by climate change
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA interprets CAA §202(a) to allow consideration of health effects that result from changes to climate caused by the air pollution (i.e., health impacts mediated by climate change), despite arguments that only direct exposure effects should be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When statutory language is ambiguous (e.g., definitions of 'public health' and 'public welfare'), adopt a reasonable interpretation that focuses on the effect on people (if the effect on people is to their health it should be considered a public health issue), and explain why the chosen interpretation is reasonable in light of the text, legislative history, and agency practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess consistency with legislative history and prior agency practice but recognize ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may consider legislative history and prior EPA actions in evaluating whether to treat indirect effects as health or welfare effects, but the text and history do not resolve the issue and do not preclude EPA's reasonable interpretive approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss relevant committee reports and past EPA assessments (e.g., ozone Criteria Document and policy assessments) to show consistency or explain differences. Make explicit when legislative history is ambiguous and why prior practice supports the current interpretive choice.
